> CFR discussion on Geopolitical dynamics in the Middle East – The interplay between Saudi Arabia, Iran, the Houthis, and Hamas

[Embedded media](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/2024/02/13/iran-celebrated-the-revolutions-45th-anniversary/embed/#?secret=nfqaqjcsBP#?secret=uDLLK79CkH)


The geopolitical dynamics in the Middle East, particularly the interplay between Saudi Arabia, Iran, the Houthis, and Hamas. It also highlights the opportunistic nature of the relationship between Iran and the Houthis, as well as the implications of the ‘axis of resistance’ against perceived Western influence. The document provides a complex and nuanced analysis of the shifting alliances and the underlying tensions that characterize the region’s politics.


the-geopolitical-dynamics-in-the-middle-eastDownload
- **The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire attempt and its failure:**The document mentions that Saudi Arabia attempted to negotiate a permanent ceasefire with the Houthis, a Yemeni group aligned with Iran, but the effort failed due to a new wave of violence following Hamas’ attack on Israel. The Houthi leader, Abdulmalik al-Houthi, expressed solidarity with Hamas, aligning himself with the ‘axis of resistance’. He threatened military action, particularly if the US intervened in support of Israel, accusing Saudi Arabia of betraying the Palestinian cause and serving as a US puppet. The document suggests that the Saudi-Houthi conflict is influenced by the broader regional dynamics and the Israeli-Palestinian issue.
- **The Iran-Houthi relationship and its regional impact:**The document explains that Iran’s support for the Houthis began in 2017, about two years into the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen, and that the relationship is seen as opportunistic rather than central to Iran’s ‘axis of resistance’. The document also notes that the extent of Iran’s influence over the Houthis is unclear, and that Iran may have limited leverage to pressure them to negotiate or to intercept their weapons shipments. The document also highlights the impact of the Houthi’s actions in the Red Sea, a vital maritime route, where they have attacked shipping and threatened to block the Bab al-Mandab strait. The document warns that these actions could trigger a broader conflict and the involvement of international powers.
- **The Saudi-Israeli relations and the Arab Peace Initiative:**The document states that Saudi Arabia has condemned Hamas’ attack on Israel and expressed its support for Egypt’s mediation efforts. It also mentions that Saudi Arabia has maintained diplomatic relations with Israel since 2018, as part of its strategy to counter Iran’s influence in the region. The document refers to the Arab Peace Initiative of 2002, which proposed a comprehensive solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on the principle of land for peace. The document argues that the initiative remains relevant and offers a framework for regional cooperation and stability.
- **The other regional conflicts involving Saudi Arabia and Iran:**The document provides a brief overview of the other regional conflicts where Saudi Arabia and Iran are on opposing sides, such as the civil war in Syria, the political crisis in Lebanon, and the unrest in Iraq. It also mentions the role of the UAE, Egypt, and Turkey in the region’s politics. The document illustrates the complexity and diversity of the Middle East’s landscape, where different actors have different interests and agendas, and where alliances are often fluid and pragmatic. The document also points out the challenges and opportunities for dialogue and cooperation among the regional players.
- **The diplomatic efforts and peacebuilding initiatives in Yemen:**The document reports that there have been significant diplomatic efforts to end the war in Yemen, such as the UN-mediated ceasefire in 2022, which brought temporary relief but failed to extend beyond six months. It also mentions recent diplomatic activities that aim to negotiate a nationwide ceasefire and address humanitarian needs, with regional efforts by Saudi Arabia and Oman playing a crucial role. It also cites some examples of successful peacebuilding initiatives in Yemen, such as the agreement signed in Beijing to de-escalate tensions, the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies’ work on dialogue and reconciliation, and the Women’s Solidarity Network’s advocacy for women’s rights and participation. The document emphasizes the need for a comprehensive and inclusive political solution that addresses the root causes of the conflict and respects the aspirations of the Yemeni people.


[Arab-Israeli wars](https://www.britannica.com/event/Arab-Israeli-wars) [https://www.youtube.com/@Search-Party](https://www.youtube.com/@Search-Party)


Also called the: October War, the Ramadan War, the Arab-Israeli war of October 1973, or the Fourth Arab-Israeli War


[Embedded media](https://www.youtube.com/embed/mBXnj_kM_cA?version=3&rel=1&showsearch=0&showinfo=1&iv_load_policy=1&fs=1&hl=en&autohide=2&wmode=transparent)


The event on October 6, 1973, referred to as the Yom Kippur War, was initiated by Egypt and Syria as a surprise attack against Israel. Here’s a brief summary:


**Yom Kippur**, most [solemn](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/solemn) of [Jewish religious holidays](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Jewish-festivals), observed on the 10th day of the lunar month of Tishri (in the course of September and October), when [Jews](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Jew-people) seek to expiate their sins and achieve reconciliation with God. Yom Kippur concludes the “10 days of repentance”


**Background**: After losing the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, and Golan Heights in the Six-Day War of 1967, Arab nations sought to regain territory. [Egyptian President Anwar el-Sadat planned a coordinated attack with Syria to alter the status quo and push for peace on more favorable terms](https://www.history.com/topics/middle-east/yom-kippur-war).


- **The Attack**: On Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, Egyptian and Syrian forces launched a coordinated assault. [Egypt attacked across the Suez Canal into the Sinai Peninsula, while Syria targeted the Golan Heights](https://www.history.com/topics/middle-east/yom-kippur-war).
- **The Response**: Israel, taken by surprise, suffered initial setbacks but eventually mobilized and repelled the invasions. With the aid of a U.S. [arms airlift, Israel regained lost territories and a cease-fire was established on October 25, 1973](https://www.history.com/topics/middle-east/yom-kippur-war).
- [**Aftermath**: The war had significant geopolitical consequences, including the start of peace negotiations between Egypt and Israel, which eventually led to the Camp David Accords](https://www.history.com/topics/middle-east/yom-kippur-war)


This conflict is a pivotal moment in Middle Eastern history, illustrating the complex interplay of military strategy, geopolitics, and the quest for peace in the region.

## 550. CFR discussion on Geopolitical dynamics in the Middle East – The interplay between Saudi Arabia, Iran, the Houthis, and Hamas

![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/saudi-arabia-and-houthies-restore-ties.jpeg?w=774)


The dynamics between Saudi Arabia, Iran, and the Houthis are central to understanding the conflict in Yemen and its broader regional implications. The Houthis, a Yemeni group aligned with Iran, have been engaged in an intense irregular warfare campaign against Saudi Arabia, using sophisticated missiles and drones. [This has led to numerous attacks on Saudi civilian targets and infrastructure, prompting Saudi military responses](https://www.csis.org/analysis/iranian-and-houthi-war-against-saudi-arabia).


[Iran’s support for the Houthis is part of a larger strategy to extend its influence across the Middle East, often referred to as the “Axis of Resistance.” This includes providing weapons, technology, and training to the Houthis, which has significantly enhanced their military capabilities](https://www.csis.org/analysis/iranian-and-houthi-war-against-saudi-arabia). The relationship between Iran and the Houthis, while not as deeply rooted as Iran’s ties with groups like Hezbollah, is nonetheless strategic, with both parties sharing opposition to Saudi Arabia and the U.S. [presence in the region](https://www.mei.edu/publications/houthis-iran-and-tensions-red-sea).


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/jointheconversation-3.jpeg?w=800)


# Israel-Hamas War: Regional Escalation and U.S. Strategy


Monday, February 12, 2024


“As Saudi Arabia attempted to negotiate a permanent ceasefire with the Houthis, a new wave of violence erupted following Hamas’ attack on Israel. Abdulmalik al-Houthi, the Houthi leader, expressed solidarity with Hamas, aligning himself with the ‘axis of resistance.’ He threatened military action, particularly if the US intervened in support of Israel, accusing Saudi Arabia of betraying the Palestinian cause and serving as a US puppet. It’s noteworthy that Iran’s support for the Houthis began in 2017, about two years into the Saudi attack, possibly due to the Houthis’ ability to trouble the Saudis. The relationship between Iran and the Houthis is seen as opportunistic rather than central to Iran’s axis of resistance. The extent to which Iran can influence the Houthis, such as in pressuring them to negotiate or intercepting shipments, remains unclear.”


The shifting alliances and the underlying tensions that characterize the Middle Eastern region’s politics.


The opportunistic nature of the relationship between Iran and the Houthis, as well as the broader implications of the ‘axis of resistance’ against perceived Western influence.

Iran was the “leading state sponsor of terrorism,” according to the State Department’s [**Country Reports**](https://www.state.gov/reports/country-reports-on-terrorism-2021/) on Terrorism 2021. The Ministry of Intelligence and Security facilitated a “wide range of terrorist and other illicit activities” in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. And the elite Quds Force – the external operations branch of the Revolutionary Guards – provided arms, training and funding to militant groups in Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen. Iran and its proxy militias posed the greatest terrorist threat in the Middle East along with ISIS and al Qaeda.


The Islamic Republic also harbored senior al Qaeda leaders despite the ideological differences between the Shiite theocracy and the Sunni jihadi movement. They found common cause in their opposition to the United States and its allies in the Middle East. The following is the 2021 Iran country report on terrorism.

## Iran


“Designated as a State Sponsor of Terrorism in 1984, Iran continued its support for terrorist-related activity in 2021, including support for Hizballah, Palestinian terrorist groups in Gaza, and various terrorist and militant groups in Iraq, Syria, Bahrain, and elsewhere throughout the Middle East. Iran used the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF) to provide support to terrorist organizations, provide cover for associated covert operations, and create instability in the region. Iran has acknowledged the involvement of the IRGC-QF in the Iraq and Syria conflicts, and the IRGC-QF is Iran’s primary mechanism for cultivating and supporting terrorist activity abroad.

Pulse of Agenda investigates the intricate interplay of factors shaping Middle Eastern geopolitics from March 2023 to January 2024, with a particular focus on the role of oil, the impacts of Iran and China Diplomacy, and potential scenarios for Middle East regional cooperation in the newly formed BRICS block.


1. [**Diverse Interests and Agendas**: The member countries have diverse political and economic systems, which can lead to conflicting interests](https://www.transcend.org/tms/2023/09/the-expansion-of-brics-challenges-and-uncertainties/)[1](https://www.transcend.org/tms/2023/09/the-expansion-of-brics-challenges-and-uncertainties/)[2](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/policy-briefs/brics-expansion-challenges-consensus-promises-influence).
2. [**Economic Dominance of China**: China’s significant economic weight within the group can overshadow the interests of other members](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/07/5-factors-limiting-the-impact-of-the-brics-nations/)[3](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/07/5-factors-limiting-the-impact-of-the-brics-nations/).
3. [**Institutionalization and Cohesion**: There are uncertainties regarding the group’s cohesion and the lack of effort towards institutionalizing the group as a cohesive unit](https://www.transcend.org/tms/2023/09/the-expansion-of-brics-challenges-and-uncertainties/)[1](https://www.transcend.org/tms/2023/09/the-expansion-of-brics-challenges-and-uncertainties/).
4. [**Consensus on Monetary Policies**: The expansion complicates achieving a consensus on economic-monetary policies, which is essential for challenging the dollar-dominated global economy](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/policy-briefs/brics-expansion-challenges-consensus-promises-influence)[2](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/policy-briefs/brics-expansion-challenges-consensus-promises-influence).
5. [**Geopolitical Tensions**: Geopolitical dynamics, such as the conflict between India and China, can hinder the group’s ability to act collectively](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/policy-briefs/brics-expansion-challenges-consensus-promises-influence)[2](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/policy-briefs/brics-expansion-challenges-consensus-promises-influence).


###### transcend.org studies.aljazeera.net


The BRICS group, which includes major emerging economies like Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, is making significant strides by inviting Middle Eastern countries to join. This move is seen as an effort to expand their influence and create a more balanced global playing field. [The countries from the Middle East that have been invited include the UAE, Egypt, Iran, and Saudi Arabia](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-755997)[1](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-755997)[2](https://theprint.ae/analysis-what-do-brics-invitations-mean-for-the-middle-east/)[3](https://alkambatimes.com/analysis-what-do-brics-invitations-mean-for-the-middle-east/)[4](https://www.iiss.org/online-analysis/online-analysis/2023/08/with-brics-expansion-china-and-middle-eastern-powers-draw-closer/).


This expansion could lead to increased cooperation and integration between BRICS and the Middle East, potentially reshaping economic and political dynamics on a global scale. [The analysis suggests that contrary to beliefs that the Middle East might become less important in the future, this region continues to hold significant strategic value](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-755997).


**Daesh’s decline:**Daesh has lost 60% of its territory and population since 2014, as it fought against multiple enemies. The Iraqi army, with US support, took Mosul, Daesh’s capital in Iraq, where it declared a caliphate in 2014. Daesh’s caliphate is near collapse as US-backed Syrian forces are closing in on Raqqa, Daesh’s capital in Syria.


These challenges highlight the complexity of BRICS’ ambition to become a more influential economic and political bloc on the global stage.

This is the final part of the documentary trilogy “Offensive”. The first-person combat footage shows the offensive actions of units of the Third Separate Assault Brigade during the summer-autumn phase of the advance of Ukrainian troops in the Bakhmut direction. Andriivka was the final point of the brigade’s offensive in Donetsk region.

After clearing the banks of the Siverskyi Donets-Donbas canal from enemy forces and entrenching in captured positions, the fighters of the brigade are starting a new stage and storming the approaches to the occupied village of Andriivka. Stormers advance from one trench to another. Grazing small arms fire and grenades going in one after another, including thermobaric ones. The occupiers are offered to surrender, but there is no time for long persuasions here, and the russians’ choice is limited – either prisoner or liquidated. “I’ll smoke you out now!”, – one of the fighters comments and continues “pouring” fire.

Thus, through the forest strips, filled with the burrows of the occupiers and fierce battles, the stormers are approaching the settlement and begin the liberation operation.

The total defeat of the enemy’s 72nd omsbr of the russian federation by the forces of the Third Assault Brigade, constant dynamics on the battlefield, the sounds of explosions, shootings and moments when you say goodbye to life, your brothers-in-arms and family. All for the sake of the victorious raising of the Ukrainian flag and the brigade banner over the liberated land. About the high price of the de-occupied territories, and what the fighters are living through at this time – in the documentary film.

The **205th Separate Cossack Motor Rifle Brigade (205 omsbr)** (Russian: 205-я отдельная мотострелковая казачья бригада) is a mechanized infantry brigade of the **Russian Ground Forces**. It is part of the **49th Combined Arms Army** and is based in **Budyonnovsk, Stavropol Krai**. [Formed in **1995** during the **First Chechen War**, this brigade has been involved in various Russian post-Soviet conflicts, including the **War of Dagestan**, **Second Chechen War**, the **Russo-Georgian War**, and the **2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/205th_Separate_Motor_Rifle_Brigade)[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/205th_Separate_Motor_Rifle_Brigade).


The **205th Brigade** was initially created by combining battalions and companies from other units. It included the **1387th**, **1393rd**, **1394th**, and **1396th Separate Motor Rifle Battalions**, as well as other supporting units. [Despite its planned base in Grozny and Shali, the brigade was continuously engaged in combat from its inception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/205th_Separate_Motor_Rifle_Brigade)[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/205th_Separate_Motor_Rifle_Brigade).


[The **205th Separate Cossack Motor Rifle Brigade** has a rich history of service in various conflicts and remains an integral part of the **Russian Ground Forces**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/205th_Separate_Motor_Rifle_Brigade)

China and Iran and Saudi Arabia diplomacy within the specified timeframe March 2023


China brokers peace cooperation recent event to end Middle East conflict between Iran and Saudi Arabia shortly before joining BRICKS


China’s role in Middle Eastern politics, particularly in relation to Iran, has been characterized by a strategic partnership that has evolved over decades. [This relationship was further highlighted when China facilitated a landmark agreement between Saudi Arabia and Iran to resume diplomatic ties and reopen embassies in March 2023](https://iranprimer.usip.org/blog/2023/mar/10/iran-and-saudi-arabia-restore-ties)[1](https://iranprimer.usip.org/blog/2023/mar/10/iran-and-saudi-arabia-restore-ties)[2](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/10/arch-rivals-iran-and-saudi-arabia-agree-to-revive-ties-reopen-embassies.html)[3](https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202303/1287105.shtml). [This move is seen as a significant step towards de-escalating tensions in the region and reflects China’s growing influence and interest in Middle Eastern affairs](https://iranprimer.usip.org/blog/2023/mar/10/iran-and-saudi-arabia-restore-ties)[4](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/china-mena-leverage-iran-houthis-yemen/).


Regarding Israel-Palestinian relations, the potential scenarios are complex and multifaceted. They include the longstanding consideration of a two-state solution, ongoing peace negotiations, regional peace initiatives, and the possibility of unilateral actions by either party. [The evolving dynamics of these relations are influenced by various factors, including international diplomacy, internal politics, and the actions of regional players](https://iranprimer.usip.org/blog/2023/mar/10/iran-and-saudi-arabia-restore-ties)[5](https://www.usip.org/publications/2020/01/israeli-palestinian-conflict-2020-what-are-possible-paths-ahead)[6](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2024/feb/07/israel-palestine-conflict-solution-peace)[7](https://medium.com/@damienbruckard/five-scenarios-for-how-the-israel-palestine-could-evolve-revisited-33eb37bfcdf5)[8](https://www.clingendael.org/sites/default/files/2023-11/CA_Scenarios_for_the_Palestinian_Issue.pdf).


The inclusion of Iran and Saudi Arabia shortly before the BRICS summit is particularly relevant, as it signifies the expanding influence of BRICS in the Middle East and the shifting geopolitical landscape. [The BRICS nations, which now include Saudi Arabia and the UAE, are emerging as key global players, indicating a multipolar world where middle powers from the Middle East are gaining prominence](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/brics-invites-uae-another-sign-multipolar-world-here)[9](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/brics-invites-uae-another-sign-multipolar-world-here)[10](https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/brics-swings-big-with-invitation-of-middle-east-countries-analysis/ar-AA1fHQYp)[11](https://themedialine.org/top-stories/brics-nations-open-door-to-middle-east-in-historic-expansion/)[12](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3232351/new-brics-members-saudi-arabia-uae-taking-step-away-us-seeking-global-roles)[13](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/brics-challenge-western-order-middle-east-how).


These developments underscore the interconnected nature of diplomacy, regional conflicts, and global alliances, shaping the political narrative of the Middle East. If you have specific aspects you’d like to explore further or other related topics you’re interested in, please let me know.


**From Microsoft Start Partners**


**China** has recently played a significant role in brokering peace cooperation between **Iran** and **Saudi Arabia**, two historic oil-producing rivals in the Middle East. After **seven years** of severed relations, the two countries have agreed to restore diplomatic ties and reopen embassies. This **historic truce**, signed in Beijing, signifies China’s newfound willingness to leverage its economic clout in third-party negotiations. President **Xi Jinping** personally participated in brokering the Iran-Saudi deal, signaling a departure from China’s former noninterventionist stance. The question now is whether China will step up to play a central role in negotiating a settlement in the **Russia-Ukraine conflict**. Reports suggest that President Xi is due to have a video call with Ukraine President **Volodymyr Zelensky**, their first direct conversation since Russia invaded Ukraine more than a year ago.

**Role of Oil in Middle Eastern Politics**


Oil plays a pivotal role in the Middle East, influencing not just the economy but also the political landscape. The region’s oil production and exportation are crucial for the global energy market. [Oil revenues significantly impact governance and international relations, often leading to a phenomenon known as the ‘resource curse,’ where oil-rich nations tend to have less economic growth and democracy compared to those without abundant natural resources](https://now.tufts.edu/2023/10/04/why-democracy-so-elusive-oil-rich-middle-east)[1](https://now.tufts.edu/2023/10/04/why-democracy-so-elusive-oil-rich-middle-east)[2](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/06/the-changing-geopolitics-of-oil-in-the-middle-east/)[3](https://www.mei.edu/publications/geopolitics-energy-transition-mena-mitigating-risks-exploring-new-opportunities).


**Climate Change Effects**


Climate change is a pressing issue in the Middle East, characterized by water scarcity, extreme weather events, and agricultural challenges. [These environmental changes have profound implications for political and social dynamics, potentially exacerbating conflicts and impacting the livelihoods of millions](https://now.tufts.edu/2023/10/04/why-democracy-so-elusive-oil-rich-middle-east)[4](https://www.omanobserver.om/article/1149351/opinion/the-climate-crucible-navigating-the-middle-easts-environmental-future)[5](https://www.mei.edu/publications/women-and-climate-change-mena-turning-adversity-opportunity)[6](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2019/04/middle-east-front-lines-climate-change-mena/)[7](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/climate-change-may-devastate-the-middle-east-heres-how-governments-should-tackle-it/).


**Scenarios for Regional Cooperation**


Regional cooperation in the Middle East can take various forms, including economic partnerships, security alliances, and environmental initiatives. [The Abraham Accords, for example, have opened new avenues for cooperation among nations in the region](https://now.tufts.edu/2023/10/04/why-democracy-so-elusive-oil-rich-middle-east)[8](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/regional-security-cooperation-partnerships-middle-east). [Diplomatic efforts to resolve conflicts also remain a critical area for collaboration, especially considering the ongoing tensions and proxy wars](https://now.tufts.edu/2023/10/04/why-democracy-so-elusive-oil-rich-middle-east)[9](https://www.mei.edu/sites/default/files/2021-10/2.%20The%20Future%20of%20Regional%20and%20International%20Dynamics%20in%20the%20Middle%20East%20.pdf)[10](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/41327/chapter/352326766).


**Other Impacting Factors**


Several other factors could influence Middle Eastern geopolitics, such as regional conflicts, diplomatic negotiations, and socio-economic developments. [The geopolitics of the region are continually reshaped by the actions of both state and non-state actors, external powers, and the shifting alliances and rivalries among countries](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-new-geopolitics-of-the-middle-east-americas-role-in-a-changing-region/)[11](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-new-geopolitics-of-the-middle-east-americas-role-in-a-changing-region/)[12](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/19448953.2021.1888251)[13](https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/FP_20190107_new_geopolitics_of_mena_final.pdf)[14](https://www.iiss.org/online-analysis/online-analysis/2023/11/the-battle-for-the-middle-easts-geopolitics/).

**Russia’s Involvement in Middle Eastern Politics**


Russia has been a significant player in Middle Eastern politics, particularly through:


- [**Military Interventions**: Notably, Russia’s military intervention in Syria since 2015 to support the Syrian government](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[1](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/).
- [**Diplomatic Initiatives**: Engaging in diplomacy with key regional states, including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[1](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/).
- [**Energy Partnerships**: Strengthening ties with Middle Eastern countries through energy agreements and projects](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/publication/report-russia-middle-east-national-security-challenges-united-states-and-israel-biden)[2](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/publication/report-russia-middle-east-national-security-challenges-united-states-and-israel-biden).


**Milestones in Turkey’s Foreign Policy**


Turkey’s foreign policy has seen several shifts, such as:


- [**NATO Relations**: While a member of NATO, Turkey has had tensions with other members due to its military operations in Syria and its purchase of Russian defense systems](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/turkeys-growing-foreign-policy-ambitions)[3](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/turkeys-growing-foreign-policy-ambitions).
- [**EU Relations**: Turkey’s EU accession process has been stalled, partly due to concerns over democratic backsliding and human rights issues](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/turkeys-growing-foreign-policy-ambitions)[3](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/turkeys-growing-foreign-policy-ambitions).
- [**Regional Relationships**: Turkey has pursued an assertive regional policy, involving military interventions in Libya and Syria, and has sought closer ties with Russia and China](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[3](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/turkeys-growing-foreign-policy-ambitions).


**Solutions to Yemen’s Crisis**


Potential solutions to Yemen’s crisis could involve:


- [**Diplomatic Efforts**: A political agreement leading to sustainable peace is seen as the long-term solution](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[4](https://yemen.un.org/en/259543-yemen-humanitarian-response-plan-hrp-2024-january-2024).
- [**Humanitarian Aid**: Coordinating the delivery of humanitarian aid and addressing the financial isolation of Yemeni banks](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[5](https://press.un.org/en/2021/sc14661.doc.htm).
- [**Military Perspective**: Ceasing the supply of weapons to warring parties and supporting truce efforts](https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2023/12/a-precarious-moment-for-yemens-truce.html)[6](https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2023/12/a-precarious-moment-for-yemens-truce.html).


**Other Regional Actors and Factors**


Other key players and factors influencing Middle Eastern geopolitics include:


- [**Saudi Arabia and Iran**: As regional rivals, their actions significantly impact the geopolitical landscape](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[7](https://www.iiss.org/online-analysis/online-analysis/2023/11/the-battle-for-the-middle-easts-geopolitics/).
- [**Non-State Actors**: Groups like Hezbollah and the Houthis play crucial roles in shaping the security dynamics of the region](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[7](https://www.iiss.org/online-analysis/online-analysis/2023/11/the-battle-for-the-middle-easts-geopolitics/).
- [**External Powers**: The United States, China, and European countries also have vested interests and influence in the Middle East](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/russia-in-the-middle-east-a-source-of-stability-or-a-pot-stirrer/)[8](https://foreignanalysis.com/where-will-global-and-regional-actors-carry-the-middle-east-in-global-shifting/).

**Red Sea Crisis**


The Red Sea crisis has significantly impacted global trade, with attacks on container vessels causing delays and additional costs. [The crisis has prompted major shipping companies to halt or reroute traffic, affecting the delivery of goods and supplies worldwide](https://www.aol.com/finance/1-million-extra-costs-weeks-162152412.html)[1](https://www.aol.com/finance/1-million-extra-costs-weeks-162152412.html)[2](https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/middle-east-crisis-live-hms-richmond-takes-over-red-sea-patrol/ar-BB1hRSLM)[3](https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/other/red-sea-crisis-hits-maersk-outlook-oversupply-will-cause-price-pressure-impact-results/ar-BB1hZLMW). [The situation escalated with Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in response to Israel’s actions in Gaza, leading to a tense military standoff in the region](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/dec/19/red-sea-shipping-crisis-bp-oil-explained-what-is-happening-and-what-does-it-mean-for-global-trade)[4](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/dec/19/red-sea-shipping-crisis-bp-oil-explained-what-is-happening-and-what-does-it-mean-for-global-trade).


**Humanitarian Impact of Yemen’s War**


Yemen’s conflict has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The war has displaced over four million people and caused widespread hunger, disease, and civilian casualties. [Despite a UN-mediated cease-fire in 2022, the combatants failed to renew the deal, leading to continued suffering and instability](https://www.aol.com/finance/1-million-extra-costs-weeks-162152412.html)[5](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/yemen-crisis)[6](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/yemen/yemen-humanitarian-needs-overview-2024-january-2024)[7](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-44466574)[8](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/yemen).


**Tensions Between Iran and Saudi Arabia**


The root causes of tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia include religious differences, power struggles, and political rivalries. [The conflict has been exacerbated by events such as the Iranian revolution, the US-led invasion of Iraq, and the Arab Spring, with both nations supporting opposing sides in regional conflicts](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-35221569)[9](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-35221569)[10](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-42008809)[11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_proxy_conflict)[12](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/article/timeline-iran-saudi-relations).


**Peace Efforts**


Recent efforts towards peace have seen Iran and Saudi Arabia restore diplomatic ties after a seven-year rift, with both countries affirming the need for regional stability and agreeing to pursue economic cooperation. **Humanitarian Impact of Yemen’s War**


Yemen’s conflict has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The war has displaced over four million people and caused widespread hunger, disease, and civilian casualties. [Despite a UN-mediated cease-fire in 2022, the combatants failed to renew the deal, leading to continued suffering and instability](https://www.aol.com/finance/1-million-extra-costs-weeks-162152412.html)[5](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/yemen-crisis)[6](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/yemen/yemen-humanitarian-needs-overview-2024-january-2024)[7](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-44466574)[8](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/yemen).

This type of missile, known as the AGM-114R9X Hellfire or “Flying Ginsu,” has been used in the past for targeted killings to reduce civilian casualties. In summary, the U.S. used a precision missile to eliminate a key militia commander in Iraq, which has led to a complex aftermath and discussions about U.S. military strategy and its implications.

- **USCENTCOM Commander’s Statement**: Gen. Michael Erik Kurilla, US CENTCOM Commander, made a statement regarding U.S. strikes in Iraq and Syria.
- **Threats to Stability**: The Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and affiliated militia groups are highlighted as direct threats to the stability of Iraq and the safety of Americans.
- **PMF’s Relationship**: The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) are formally under the command of the Iraqi prime minister but have ties with Iran and the IRGC.
- **Recent Strikes**: The U.S. strikes targeted the PMF’s mobile headquarters in the al Qaim district, Anbar province, impacting elements of the 13th and 45th PMF Brigades.

**PRESS RELEASE** | Feb. 7, 2024


# USCENTCOM Conducts Strike Killing Kata’ib Hezbollah Senior Leader


**USCENTCOM**


February 07, 2024
Release Number 20240207-01
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE


**TAMPA, Fla.** – At 9:30 p.m. (Baghdad time) February 7, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces conducted a unilateral strike in Iraq in response to the attacks on U.S. service members, killing a Kata’ib Hezbollah commander responsible for directly planning and participating in attacks on U.S. forces in the region.


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/instability-in-iraq.png?w=853)


There are no indications of collateral damage or civilian casualties at this time. The United States will continue to take necessary action to protect our people. We will not hesitate to hold responsible all those who threaten our forces’ safety.


What is the Popular Mobilization Forces? Why did the US strike in Iraq and Syria? Who are some of Iran’s allies in the region?


The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also known as Al-Hashd Al-Shaabi, is an Iraqi state-sponsored umbrella organization composed of various armed factions, predominantly Shia Muslim groups, but also including Sunni Muslim, Christian, and Yazidi groups. [Formed in 2014, the PMF has fought in major battles against ISIL and includes factions with ideologies ranging from Shia Islamism to anti-Americanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces)[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces).


The US strikes in Iraq and Syria were in response to a drone attack in Jordan that killed three American soldiers. [The US targeted facilities associated with the PMF and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), aiming to degrade their capabilities and prevent further attacks](https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/us-strikes-targets-in-iraq-and-syria-after-middle-east-drone-attack-kills-three-soldiers/ar-BB1hGR8P)[2](https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/us-strikes-targets-in-iraq-and-syria-after-middle-east-drone-attack-kills-three-soldiers/ar-BB1hGR8P)[3](https://apnews.com/article/iraq-syria-strikes-hamas-militia-iran-us-62be7c7b500de1d0f1287a9b2c6f82dc).


Iran’s allies in the region include state actors like Syria and non-state actors such as Hezbollah. [These allies have been involved in various conflicts and have supported Iran’s regional objectives, often opposing US interests](https://www.csmonitor.com/text_edition/World/Middle-East/2024/0206/US-confronts-Axis-Who-are-Iran-s-allies-Can-they-be-deterred)[4](https://www.csmonitor.com/text_edition/World/Middle-East/2024/0206/US-confronts-Axis-Who-are-Iran-s-allies-Can-they-be-deterred)[5](https://www.cfr.org/article/irans-regional-armed-network).

CSISQ&A / MIDDLE EAST & NORTH AFRICA


Regional tensions from over. CSISQ&A / MIDDLE EAST & NORTH AFRICA Understanding the Risks of U.S.-Iran Escalation amid the Gaza Conflict Terrible as the Gaza war’s toll has already been, it would get worse if sustained fighting were to erupt between the U.S. and Iran or its Middle East allies. Crisis Group experts Brian Finucane, Lahib Higel, Naysan Rafati and Ali Vaez lay out the dangers.


The selected text refers to the potential risks of an escalation between the U.S. and Iran, particularly in the context of the ongoing conflict in Gaza. The Crisis Group experts mentioned—Brian Finucane, Lahib Higel, Naysan Rafati, and Ali Vaez—have discussed the implications of such an escalation. [They warn that the already devastating toll of the Gaza war could worsen if it leads to broader conflict involving the U.S., Iran, and their respective allies in the Middle East](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-united-states/understanding-risks-us-iran)[1](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-united-states/understanding-risks-us-iran).


The situation is complex, with various incidents contributing to the tensions. For instance, there have been attacks involving drones and indirect fire on U.S. forces based in Iraq and Syria, with Iran-backed groups in Iraq claiming responsibility. These attacks occurred amid a build-up of U.S. [military assets in the region as Israel continued its offensive in the Gaza Strip](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-united-states/understanding-risks-us-iran)[1](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-united-states/understanding-risks-us-iran).


Moreover, the Houthis in Yemen have promised escalation after U.S. and British strikes targeted sites used by the Iranian-backed militant group. [The strikes were a response to Houthi attacks on military and commercial vessels in the Red Sea, and the Houthis have stated that their attacks will not cease until Israel’s assault on Gaza ends](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2024/02/04/israel-hamas-war-news-gaza-palestine/)[2](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2024/02/04/israel-hamas-war-news-gaza-palestine/).


[The end of a fragile ceasefire between Hamas and Israel in Gaza has also reignited tensions, with clashes taking place amid the Israeli military’s offensive on the Gaza strip, raising concerns about a broader regional conflict](https://english.elpais.com/international/2023-12-05/us-iran-tensions-escalate-in-the-shadow-of-gaza-war.html)[3](https://english.elpais.com/international/2023-12-05/us-iran-tensions-escalate-in-the-shadow-of-gaza-war.html).


In summary, the selected text highlights the grave concerns of potential U.S.-Iran escalation amid the Gaza conflict, which could lead to a more extensive and destructive regional war.

Liwa al-Tafuf, also known as the 13th brigade of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), is a militia group operating primarily in Iraq and Syria. It has been designated as a terrorist organization by some entities due to its involvement in armed conflict and alleged ties to extremist activities.


Liwa al-Tafuf, the 13th brigade of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), is indeed a militia group active in Iraq and Syria. It’s part of the PMF, an Iraqi state-sponsored umbrella organization composed of various armed factions. Liwa al-Tafuf is particularly noted for its logistical and administrative support to military operations against U.S. [forces in the region](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/profile-liwa-al-tafuf-13th-pmf-brigade)[1](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/profile-liwa-al-tafuf-13th-pmf-brigade). The brigade has been involved in significant battles against the Islamic State and has a history of association with Kataib Hezbollah, a group known for facilitating anti-U.S. [attacks](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/profile-liwa-al-tafuf-13th-pmf-brigade)[1](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/profile-liwa-al-tafuf-13th-pmf-brigade).


The PMF itself is a complex entity with a diverse composition, including Shia, Sunni, Christian, and Yazidi groups, and has been a key player in the fight against ISIL. [However, many of its main militias have origins tracing back to groups that previously fought against the United States and Coalition forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces)[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces).


In summary, Liwa al-Tafuf is recognized for its role in regional conflicts and its connections to broader militia activities within the PMF framework. It has garnered attention and designation as a terrorist organization by some due to its actions and affiliations.

- **US strikes in Iraq and Syria**: On February 2, 2024, the US launched a series of airstrikes targeting Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and Iran-backed militia groups in Iraq and Syria, in retaliation for a drone attack that killed three US soldiers in Jordan. [The US used 125 precision-guided missiles to hit 85 targets, including command and control centers, rockets, missiles, and drones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_2024_United_States_airstrikes_in_Iraq_and_Syria)[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_2024_United_States_airstrikes_in_Iraq_and_Syria).

[Iran also fired several missiles at US bases and facilities in Iraq, Syria, and Pakistan, causing some damage but no casualties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_2024_United_States_airstrikes_in_Iraq_and_Syria)[2](https://time.com/6555803/iran-us-consulate-iraq-attack-israel/).
- **US and UK operation in Yemen**: On February 7, 2024, the US and UK conducted joint air and missile strikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are supported by Iran and have been launching attacks on ships in the Red Sea bound for Israel. [The US and UK used cruise missiles and drones to hit eight Houthi targets, including radars and missile sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_missile_strikes_in_Yemen)[3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_missile_strikes_in_Yemen).

Title: “The PMF and Its Iranian Ties: Implications for US-Iraq Relations”


The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in Iraq, formally under the command of the Iraqi prime minister, are significantly influenced by Iran and its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).


Recently, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Faleh al Fayyadh, the leader of the PMF, citing his involvement in human rights abuses and violence against Iraqi protesters.


In response, Fayyadh denounced the sanctions as a violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, while Iran condemned them, reaffirming its support for the PMF in combating terrorism and safeguarding Iraq’s security.


These sanctions have exacerbated tensions between the US and Iraq, already strained by the killing of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani and PMF commander Abu Mahdi al Muhandis by US forces in January 2020. The Iraqi government has called for the withdrawal of US troops, and some PMF factions have threatened to target US interests in Iraq.


The fallout from these sanctions could impact the formation of Iraq’s new cabinet, which has been delayed by political disputes and protests. Fayyadh, a close ally of former Prime Minister Nouri al Maliki, holds influence within the largest parliamentary bloc. The sanctions may either weaken Fayyadh’s political standing or bolster his support among his backers.


These developments underscore the complex interplay between regional powers, Iraqi politics, and US involvement in the region, with potential ramifications for stability and security in Iraq and beyond.

The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also known as Al-Hashd Al-Shaabi, is an Iraqi state-sponsored umbrella organization composed of various armed factions. While it is formally under the command of the Iraqi prime minister, it has significant ties to Iran and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). [These ties have led to concerns about the PMF’s influence on Iraq’s sovereignty and its role in regional conflicts](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-popular-mobilization-force-is-turning-iraq-into-an-iranian-client-state/)[1](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-popular-mobilization-force-is-turning-iraq-into-an-iranian-client-state/)[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces).


The PMF was formed in response to the ISIS threat in 2014 and has since become a key player in Iraq’s security landscape. However, its alignment with Iran-aligned factions has raised questions about its autonomy and the potential for it to act in Iran’s interests, particularly against U.S. [forces and allies in the region](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-popular-mobilization-force-is-turning-iraq-into-an-iranian-client-state/)[3](https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2024-01-18/explainer-iran-and-its-proxies-and-widening-violence-in-the-middle-east)[4](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/new-vulnerabilities-for-iraqs-resilient-popular-mobilization-forces/).


[The PMF’s relationship with Iran and the IRGC underscores the complex dynamics of power and influence in Iraq, where state and non-state actors often intersect, and foreign interests can play a significant role in domestic affairs](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-popular-mobilization-force-is-turning-iraq-into-an-iranian-client-state/)[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces).


In summary, the PMF is a paramilitary force in Iraq with strong ties to Iran and the IRGC, which impacts its operations and the broader security context in the Middle East.

## 560. Unmanned News – Pulse of Agenda

- **Post ID:** 307
- **Date:** 2024-02-06T19:31:02
- **URL:** https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/2024/02/06/unmanned-news-pulse-of-agenda/
- **Slug:** unmanned-news-pulse-of-agenda
- **source_id:** SRC-WP-307

![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/iraq-mobilization-forces-3.jpg?w=720)


The PMF’s 13th brigade (Liwa al-Tafuf) was formed by splintered-off commanders from the Ali al-Sistani–loyalist PMF 11th brigade (Liwa Ali al-Akbar) in 2014. The new brigade was formed around a former head of security for the Karbala shrines named Qasim Muslih. Liwa al-Tafuf retained some support and drew some legitimacy from being connected to the shrines and to Sistani, but it quickly ceased to be a real “*atabat*” (shrine) PMF unit and instead fell increasingly under the administrative influence and operational control of [Kataib Hezbollah](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/node/16641) founder and U.S.-designated terrorist Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, then operational commander of the PMF.


The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) is a state-sponsored umbrella organization that includes various militia groups in Iraq. Some of these groups are aligned with Iran and have been involved in attacks against U.S. interests and personnel. One of these groups is the 13th brigade, also known as Liwa al-Tafuf, which has a complicated history and relationship with the PMF and its leadership.


Liwa al-Tafuf was formed by commanders who split from the 11th brigade (Liwa Ali al-Akbar), a PMF unit that was loyal to the influential Shia cleric Ali al-Sistani, who is widely respected by Iraqis for his moderate and pragmatic stance. The 11th brigade was established to protect the holy shrines in Karbala and Najaf, and to follow Sistani’s fatwa to fight against the Islamic State.


However, some of the commanders of the 11th brigade were dissatisfied with Sistani’s authority and influence over the PMF, and decided to form their own brigade, Liwa al-Tafuf, under the leadership of Qasim Muslih, a former security head for the Karbala shrines. Muslih was close to Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, the founder of Kataib Hezbollah, a U.S.-designated terrorist group and one of the most powerful and radical factions within the PMF. Al-Muhandis was also the operational commander of the PMF until he was killed by a U.S. drone strike in January 2020, along with Iranian general Qasem Soleimani.


Under Muslih and al-Muhandis, Liwa al-Tafuf became more militant and aggressive, and adopted the ideology and tactics of Kataib Hezbollah. It participated in attacks against U.S. forces and facilities in Iraq, and supported Iran’s regional agenda. It also clashed with other PMF factions that were loyal to Sistani or the Iraqi government, such as the 9th brigade (Liwa Abbas al-Akbar) and the 1st brigade (Liwa al-Imam Ali).


The case of Liwa al-Tafuf illustrates the complex dynamics within the PMF, and the challenges that the Iraqi government faces in dealing with this heterogeneous and influential force. The PMF has played a crucial role in defeating the Islamic State and filling the security vacuum in many areas of Iraq, but it has also been a source of instability and violence, especially due to its Iranian-backed elements. The Iraqi government has tried to reform and integrate the PMF into the state security apparatus, but it has faced resistance and backlash from some of its leaders and supporters.


The future of Liwa al-Tafuf and other PMF factions will depend on several factors, such as the political situation in Iraq, the U.S.-Iran tensions, and the role of Sistani and other religious authorities. The PMF is not a monolithic entity, but a diverse and dynamic one that reflects the diversity and dynamism of Iraq itself.

A veteran diplomat and former deputy foreign minister, Amir-Abdollahian was appointed as Iran’s foreign minister by the newly elected president Ebrahim Raisi in August 2021.


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/iran_president_ebrahim_raisi.jpeg?w=1024)


Amir-Abdollahian is known as a hardliner and a staunch supporter of Iran’s regional policies and proxy groups, such as Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen. He is also an expert on Arab affairs and has extensive contacts and experience in dealing with the countries of the Middle East and North Africa. Amir-Abdollahian’s mission is to restore Iran’s diplomatic relations and credibility with its neighbors and the international community, while also pursuing Iran’s national interests and rights, particularly regarding the nuclear deal and the sanctions imposed by the US and its allies. Amir-Abdollahian has a close and trusting relationship with Raisi, who shares his conservative and anti-Western outlook and his commitment to the principles of the Islamic Revolution. Raisi has delegated Amir-Abdollahian with the responsibility and authority to lead Iran’s foreign policy and negotiations and has expressed his confidence and support for his performance and achievements.


Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud is the current Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia. He has been serving in this position since October 23, 2019, following his appointment by King Salman. Born on November 1, 1974, in Frankfurt, West Germany, Prince Faisal is a member of the House of Saud and has a background in business administration, which he studied at King Saud University. [Before becoming Foreign Minister, he served as an adviser at the Saudi Arabian Embassy in the US and held senior positions in Saudi and international companies, especially in the aerospace and weapons sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Farhan_Al_Saud)

Prince Faisal is known for his diplomatic skills and fluency in German, which stems from his early years spent in Germany. Faisal Al Saud is a well-established diplomat and politician who has been contributing to Saudi Arabia’s international relations since his appointment as the Foreign Minister.

China’s diplomacy with Iran and Saudi Arabia is multifaceted, reflecting its strategic interests in the Middle East.


**With Iran**, China has a longstanding partnership that has evolved over 40 years, particularly since the Iran-Iraq War. [This relationship is crucial for China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in the region and provides Iran with vital economic support amidst international sanctions](https://thediplomat.com/2021/12/the-china-iran-strategic-partnership-40-years-in-the-making/)[1](https://thediplomat.com/2021/12/the-china-iran-strategic-partnership-40-years-in-the-making/). [China’s involvement in Iran also includes public diplomacy efforts and offers of mediation in regional conflicts](https://thediplomat.com/2021/12/the-china-iran-strategic-partnership-40-years-in-the-making/)[2](https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/china-and-iran-push-public-diplomacy-but-will-beijing-s-soft-power-tactics-work-in-the-islamic-republic/ar-BB1he4ev)[3](https://thediplomat.com/2024/01/trouble-among-neighbors-iran-pakistan-and-chinas-offer-of-mediation/). The partnership challenges U.S. [hegemony and has implications for global geopolitics, especially considering Iran’s use of proxy forces in the Middle East](https://thediplomat.com/2021/12/the-china-iran-strategic-partnership-40-years-in-the-making/)[4](https://thediplomat.com/2024/02/the-iran-factor-in-the-china-taiwan-us-triangle/).


[**With Saudi Arabia**, China’s relationship is under pressure due to regional tensions but remains strong, driven by mutual economic interests and policy initiatives like Saudi Vision 2030 and the BRI](https://thediplomat.com/2023/11/china-and-saudi-arabia-a-partnership-under-pressure/)[5](https://thediplomat.com/2023/11/china-and-saudi-arabia-a-partnership-under-pressure/). [China supports Saudi Arabia’s role in international and regional affairs and coordinates on Middle Eastern issues to promote regional peace and stability](https://thediplomat.com/2021/12/the-china-iran-strategic-partnership-40-years-in-the-making/)[6](https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/zxxx_662805/202211/t20221101_10795076.html). [The partnership has faced challenges, such as the recent conflict in Gaza, which has raised concerns for investors and the international community](https://thediplomat.com/2023/11/china-and-saudi-arabia-a-partnership-under-pressure/)[5](https://thediplomat.com/2023/11/china-and-saudi-arabia-a-partnership-under-pressure/).


In summary, China’s diplomacy with both Iran and Saudi Arabia is characterized by strategic partnerships that serve economic, geopolitical, and security interests, while also navigating the complexities of regional politics and U.S. relations.

One of the most significant changes in the Iranian military and political landscape was the transition from Jafari to Salami as the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in 2019. The IRGC is a powerful branch of the armed forces that has influence over various domains of Iran’s domestic and foreign policy, including its nuclear program, ballistic missile development, regional proxy wars, and internal security. The IRGC leader is appointed by the Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who is the ultimate authority in Iran’s theocratic system.


Salami replaced Jafari, who had led the IRGC for over a decade, and who had a more conservative and cautious approach to the security and stability of Iran and the region. Jafari was seen as a loyal but passive follower of Khamenei, who did not take any major initiatives or risks without the approval of the Supreme Leader. Jafari was also wary of escalating tensions with the United States and its allies in the Gulf, and he preferred to maintain a low profile and avoid direct confrontation.


Salami, on the other hand, has a more hands-on and aggressive approach to the security and stability of Iran and the region. He is loyal to Khamenei and follows the humani ideology, which is a branch of Shia Islam that believes in the imminent return of the Mahdi, the hidden imam who will bring justice and peace to the world. Salami views Khamenei as the representative of the Mahdi on earth, and he considers himself as the executor of Khamenei’s will. Salami is willing to take more risks and challenge the status quo in the region.

The Complex Dynamics of Iran’s Political Landscape: A Tale of Assassinations and Power Struggles


In Iran, the political system diverges significantly from those of many other countries. Unlike in most nations, where the head of state holds paramount importance, in Iran, Ayatollahs, major religious leaders, play a pivotal role in shaping the country’s destiny. While an Ayatollah’s primary position is religious, it also extends to a central role in politics, influencing state matters and even participating in the selection of state leaders. Currently, Ayatollah Khomeini holds the authority to appoint key state figures, exerting influence over presidential elections and eligibility criteria for candidates.


Against this backdrop, a covert war is unfolding involving the United States, Israel, and Iran—a proxy war characterized by conflicts taking place far from the nations’ own territories. In this ongoing struggle, individuals closely associated with Ayatollah Khomeini are being systematically assassinated. This complex geopolitical chess game revolves around two crucial policies for Iran: nuclear armament and expanding its sphere of control in the region.


The responsibility for executing these policies fell upon two influential figures, Mossen Fakhrizadeh and Qassem Suleimani. Suleimani, the commander of the Revolutionary Guard, and Fakhrizadeh, recognized as one of Khamenei’s closest confidants, played instrumental roles in implementing Iran’s nuclear ambitions and expanding its influence in the Middle East, respectively.


Suleimani, considered a legend among the Iranian people, met his demise in a drone attack on January 3rd, following a meeting with government officials in Iraq. In response, Iran declared a period of national mourning and issued a stern warning against the unchecked assassinations. However, the absence of retaliation seemingly emboldened the attackers, leading to the subsequent assassination of Fakhrizadeh.


The decision to target Fakhrizadeh was reportedly based on intelligence seized by Israel’s agency, Mossad, during a 2018 operation in Iran. Documents identified him as the key figure behind Iran’s nuclear program, making his elimination crucial for regional power dynamics. Israel, in its quest to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran, had already engaged in cyber-attacks and sabotage against Iranian nuclear facilities.


The assassinations of these figures, under constant protection, required highly sophisticated methods. Fakhrizadeh, an insider in Iran, enjoyed continuous protection from Iranian intelligence. The Mossad meticulously planned the operation for eight months, assembling a team of over 20 agents, including Israelis and Iranians, to monitor Fakhrizadeh’s movements.


The actual assassination occurred on a Friday as Fakhrizadeh traveled to his villa in eastern Tehran. A remote-controlled weapon, weighing a ton with integrated explosives, was deployed along his known route. The weapon was remotely fired by agents, resulting in Fakhrizadeh’s death by 13 bullets. The integrated bomb destroyed evidence, and the Mossad team swiftly fled the scene, leaving Iran without detection.


As prominent figures close to Ayatollah Khomeini continue to be targeted and eliminated, there is a growing sense of isolation around Khamenei in Iran. The question that looms large is whether these calculated assassinations will persist, further reshaping the intricate political landscape of the region.

Centcom – U.S. Forces, Allies Conduct Joint Strikes in Yemen
USCENTCOM Security Brief| Feb. 3, 2024

Overview
· The US Forces and the UK Armed Forces are close allies and partners in various military operations and missions around the world.
· They share common values, interests, and objectives in promoting global security, stability, and democracy.
· They cooperate in various domains, such as intelligence, cyber, nuclear, space, and special operations.

US and UK Forces: The US Forces and the UK Armed Forces are allies and partners in various military operations and missions around the world. They share common values, interests, and objectives in promoting global security, stability, and democracy.
Cooperation in different domains: The US and Allied Forces cooperate in various domains, such as intelligence, cyber, nuclear, space, and special operations. They exchange information, resources, and expertise to enhance their capabilities and effectiveness.
Current operations in the Red Sea: The US and Allied Forces have been conducting operations in the Red Sea to counter the threat posed by the Houthis, a rebel group in Yemen that is backed by Iran. The Houthis have been launching attacks on civilian and commercial vessels in the strategic waterway, using drones and missiles supplied by Tehran. The US and Allied Forces have responded by targeting the Houthis’ missile and drone launch sites, as well as their command-and-control centers, with precision airstrikes. The aim of these operations is to deter further attacks and protect the freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, which is vital for global trade and energy security.

A joint operation by US Forces and the armed forces of the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, and New Zealand destroyed 36 military targets in 13 locations held by the houthis, a group backed by Iran. The houthis’ arsenals, air defenses, and headquarters were wiped out by the continuous attack. The multi-target air strikes that happened at the same time caught the armed group in Yemen off guard. The United States attacked many underground storage facilities, command and control centers, missile systems, drone storage, and operational locations as part of their mission. F-18s successfully hit and destroyed houthi drone bases in the Hodeida port area during multi-domain operations last Saturday afternoon. Around 90 ships were sailing through the Red Sea waters hours before the latest air strikes against houthi positions on February 03, 2024

[Embedded media](https://www.youtube.com/embed/xNJrho9t9LI?version=3&rel=1&showsearch=0&showinfo=1&iv_load_policy=1&fs=1&hl=en&autohide=2&wmode=transparent)


By Manus Cranny – – Bloomberg Television October 27,2023 [https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2023-10-28/iran-foreign-minister-on-syria-stability-in-region-video](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2023-10-28/iran-foreign-minister-on-syria-stability-in-region-video)


In a recent interview with Bloomberg, Iran’s Foreign Minister Hossein Amir Abdollahian reiterated his country’s support for the Syrian government and its readiness to send more troops if needed. He also warned Israel that a ground invasion of Syria would have grave consequences for the region and its own security.


Amirabdollahian, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly, said that Iran has been providing military and humanitarian assistance to Syria since the start of the civil war in 2011. He said that Iran respects Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and does not seek to impose its will on the Syrian people.


He also said that Iran is open to dialogue with other regional and international actors to find a political solution to the Syrian crisis, but he stressed that any such solution must respect the will of the Syrian people and their legitimate government.


However, he also expressed his concern about the increasing threats from Israel, which has repeatedly bombed Iranian and Syrian targets in Syria. He said that Israel is playing with fire and risking a wider war in the region. He warned that if Israel launches a ground invasion of Syria, Iran will not stand idly by and will respond with full force.


He said that Iran does not want war, but it will defend its interests and allies in the region. He urged Israel to respect international law and refrain from further aggression. He also called on the US and other Western countries to stop supporting Israel’s violations and to pressure it to end its occupation of Palestinian lands.


He said that Iran believes that peace and stability in the region can only be achieved through dialogue and cooperation, not through violence and intimidation. He said that Iran is ready to work with all countries that share this vision and respect its rights.

# Israel says it has struck more than 50 Hezbollah targets in Syria since Oct 7


Story by Reuters • 1d [https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/israel-says-it-has-struck-more-than-50-hezbollah-targets-in-syria-since-oct-7/ar-BB1hIVgS?ocid=socialshare](https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/israel-says-it-has-struck-more-than-50-hezbollah-targets-in-syria-since-oct-7/ar-BB1hIVgS?ocid=socialshare)


Israeli soldiers take part in training session near the Israel border with Syria at the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, February 1, 2024. REUTERS/Gil Eliyahu/File Photo© Thomson Reuters


JERUSALEM (Reuters) -The Israeli military said on Saturday that since the outbreak of the Gaza war on Oct. 7 it had struck more than 50 targets in Syria linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese movement Hezbollah.


The remarks, in a briefing by chief military spokesperson Rear Admiral Daniel Hagari that mainly discussed efforts to beat back Hezbollah attacks launched in solidarity with Hamas, were a departure from Israel’s usual reticence about Syria operations.


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/syria-linked-to-the-iranian-backed-lebanese-movement-hezbollah.jpeg?w=612)


“Everywhere Hezbollah is, we shall be. We will take action everywhere required in the Middle East,” Hagari said.


Israeli forces have attacked 34,000 Hezbollah targets in Lebanon, including 120 border surveillance outposts, 40 caches of missiles and other weaponry and more than 40 command centres, Hagari said. He put the number of enemy dead at more than 200.


Hagari said Israel had deployed three army divisions along its side of the Lebanese border in anticipation of Hezbollah getting involved after Palestinian Hamas launched a shock cross-border attack on Oct. 7, triggering the war in the Gaza Strip.


With tens of thousands of its northern residents having evacuated, Israel has threatened to escalate the Lebanon fighting unless Hezbollah backs off from the border – and has sought Western help in finding a diplomatic solution in Beirut.


(Writing by Dan WilliamsEditing by Mark Potter)

![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/iraq-mobilization-forces-1.jpg?w=720)


**Militia Spotlight: Profiles** is a series by **The Washington Institute** that provides concise profiles for major Iraqi militia entities. These profiles offer basic data, including the entity’s name, logo, and type of activity. They also summarize the best available evidence regarding the entity’s history, alignment, and relationships with other groups. The goal is to assist journalists and government analysts in understanding the connections between these armed groups. [The profiles are regularly updated and serve as a repository of institutional memory on various armed groups associated with Iraqi militias](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/series/militia-spotlight-profiles)[1](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/series/militia-spotlight-profiles).


Additionally, **How to Use Militia Spotlight: Profiles** offers short, quickly digestible profiles that provide background information on militia-related organizations. [Each profile answers three key questions: the name of the entity, its English-language meaning, its logo, and a description of its nature and activities](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/how-use-militia-spotlight-profiles)[2](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/how-use-militia-spotlight-profiles).


[In summary, **Militia Spotlight: Profiles** provides valuable insights into the major Iraqi militia entities, aiding in understanding their affiliations and track records](https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/series/militia-spotlight-profiles)

## 565. Qaani’s appointment by Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei

![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/d8add8b3db8cd986_d8b3d984d8a7d985db8c2-1.jpg?w=345)


The final say in all matters of state and religion in Iran, Khamenei has a close relationship with Qaani, who is a loyal follower of his ideology and vision. Khamenei trusts Qaani to execute his orders and maintain his authority, especially in the face of internal and external challenges. Khamenei also views Qaani as a reliable and competent commander, who can manage the Quds force and its operations in a pragmatic and effective way. Khamenei expects Qaani to continue Soleimani’s legacy of advancing Iran’s interests and influence in the region, but also to avoid unnecessary risks and conflicts that could endanger Iran’s security and stability. Khamenei has given Qaani his full backing and support, and has urged him to work closely with other military and political leaders in Iran.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Hossein Amir-Abdollahian mission of diplomacy and appointment by Iranian President Raisi. Who is Saudi Arabia’s new foreign minister Faisal Al Saud?


Iran and Saudi Arabia have historically had a complex relationship, marked by both cooperation and rivalry. The recent diplomatic breakthrough, with both countries agreeing to resume diplomatic ties, is a significant development in the geopolitics of the Middle East. Here’s a high-level overview of how they might be engaging in geopolitical diplomacy discussions:


1. [**Restoration of Diplomatic Relations**: The first step is the mutual decision to restore diplomatic relations, which can lead to reopening embassies and starting formal diplomatic communication](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian)[1](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian).
2. [**Addressing Regional Conflicts**: Both countries could discuss ways to de-escalate tensions and resolve conflicts in the region where they have competing interests, such as in Yemen and Syria](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/iran-saudi-arabia-diplomacy-why-it-matters-israel-lebanon-yemen-iraq-middle-east/)[2](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/iran-saudi-arabia-diplomacy-why-it-matters-israel-lebanon-yemen-iraq-middle-east/).
3. [**Economic Cooperation**: They might explore opportunities for economic collaboration, especially considering the global energy market and potential trade agreements](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian)[1](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian).
4. [**Cultural and Religious Dialogue**: As two major Islamic countries representing different sects, they could engage in interfaith dialogue to promote religious tolerance and unity](https://uscpublicdiplomacy.org/blog/iran-saudi-arabia-honeymoon-how-public-diplomacy-can-sustain-peace-between-tehran-and-riyadh)[3](https://uscpublicdiplomacy.org/blog/iran-saudi-arabia-honeymoon-how-public-diplomacy-can-sustain-peace-between-tehran-and-riyadh).
5. [**International Mediation**: The involvement of a third party, like China, can facilitate discussions and help maintain momentum in the diplomatic process](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian)[1](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian).
6. [**Public Diplomacy**: Leveraging media and public statements to shape a positive narrative around the rapprochement and its benefits for regional stability](https://uscpublicdiplomacy.org/blog/iran-saudi-arabia-honeymoon-how-public-diplomacy-can-sustain-peace-between-tehran-and-riyadh)[3](https://uscpublicdiplomacy.org/blog/iran-saudi-arabia-honeymoon-how-public-diplomacy-can-sustain-peace-between-tehran-and-riyadh).
7.


These discussions are likely to be complex and multifaceted, involving a range of issues from security to economic development, and will require sustained effort from both sides to achieve lasting peace and cooperation in the region. The role of international mediators and the global context will also be crucial in shaping the outcomes of these discussions.


Learn more[1crisisgroup.org](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran-saudi-arabia/impact-saudi-iranian)


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/foreign-minister-of-iran-1.jpeg?w=367)


A veteran diplomat and former deputy foreign minister, Amir-Abdollahian was appointed as Iran’s foreign minister by the newly elected president Ebrahim Raisi in August 2021.


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/iran_president_ebrahim_raisi.jpeg?w=1024)


Amir-Abdollahian is known as a hardliner and a staunch supporter of Iran’s regional policies and proxy groups, such as Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen. He is also an expert on Arab affairs and has extensive contacts and experience in dealing with the countries of the Middle East and North Africa. Amir-Abdollahian’s mission is to restore Iran’s diplomatic relations and credibility with its neighbors and the international community, while also pursuing Iran’s national interests and rights, particularly regarding the nuclear deal and the sanctions imposed by the US and its allies. Amir-Abdollahian has a close and trusting relationship with Raisi, who shares his conservative and anti-Western outlook and his commitment to the principles of the Islamic Revolution. Raisi has delegated Amir-Abdollahian with the responsibility and authority to lead Iran’s foreign policy and negotiations and has expressed his confidence and support for his performance and achievements.


Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud is the current Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia. He has been serving in this position since October 23, 2019, following his appointment by King Salman. Born on November 1, 1974, in Frankfurt, West Germany, Prince Faisal is a member of the House of Saud and has a background in business administration, which he studied at King Saud University. [Before becoming Foreign Minister, he served as an adviser at the Saudi Arabian Embassy in the US and held senior positions in Saudi and international companies, especially in the aerospace and weapons sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Farhan_Al_Saud)


![](https://jessrsdincyahoocom.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/prince-faisal-bin-farhan-al-saud.jpg?w=330)


Prince Faisal is known for his diplomatic skills and fluency in German, which stems from his early years spent in Germany. [His political career includes roles such as the Saudi Ambassador to Germany and an adviser to the Royal Court of Saudi Arabia1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Farhan_Al_Saud). [He is recognized for using his command of English and social media presence to promote Saudi Arabia’s foreign policy internationally](https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/saudi/who-is-saudi-arabias-new-foreign-minister-faisal-al-saud-1.67354918)


Faisal Al Saud is a well-established diplomat and politician who has been contributing to Saudi Arabia’s international relations since his appointment as the Foreign Minister.
